medications.drug: amoxicillin 875 MG / clavulanate 125 MG Oral Tablet
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth twice daily for 10 days

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text:
CT ABDOMEN AND PELVIS WITH IV CONTRAST. IV fluids given before and after per renal protocol.
Clinical: LLQ pain, fever. History of pancreaticoduodenectomy.
Findings: Pericolic fat stranding around the sigmoid colon with a short segment of bowel wall thickening. No abscess. No free air. Postsurgical changes of pancreaticoduodenectomy without mass. Liver, spleen, adrenal glands and kidneys unremarkable. No hydronephrosis. Bladder normal. No enlarged nodes. No ascites.
reports.conclusion: Acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis. No abscess or perforation.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN RECORD
Patient: Thomas Casey, 71 M. Arrived 06/20/2024 13:40.

CC: left lower belly pain x 3 days.

HPI: Dull, steady ache low on the left, getting worse over three days, with a low-grade fever, nausea and not much appetite. Looser stools the past two days. No vomiting, no bright red blood, no dark tarry stools. Has had a couple of milder bouts of this before that went away on their own; this one will not let up.
PMH: pancreatic adenocarcinoma resected 2022 with chemo afterward; CKD stage 3 from diabetic kidney disease; diabetes; hypertension; glaucoma; bullous pemphigoid. Colonoscopy in 2016, normal.
Meds: metformin, lisinopril, HCTZ, atorvastatin, pancrelipase, latanoprost. NKDA.
Social: never smoker, occasional wine.

Triage vitals: T 38.2 C (100.8 F), BP 128/74, HR 94.
Exam: uncomfortable but nontoxic. Abdomen tender in the LLQ, no rebound, no guarding. Bowel sounds a bit decreased. Rectal: normal tone, no mass, brown stool.

Labs: WBC elevated. Creatinine at his baseline. Urinalysis without signs of infection or blood.
CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast (renal hydration protocol): sigmoid fat stranding and wall thickening, no abscess, no free air.

Dx: acute sigmoid diverticulitis, uncomplicated.
Dispo: tolerating oral fluids, pain controlled with acetaminophen. Discharged home on amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 10 days, clear liquids advancing to low-residue diet. Return for worsening pain, high fever, vomiting or bleeding. Follow up with PCP within 1 week; consider colonoscopy after recovery.

Emergency Medicine

Seen in the ED 6/20 for sigmoid diverticulitis on CT (history from patient and the CT report, which is in our system; ED physician note requested). On day 7 of 10 of amoxicillin-clavulanate. Pain mostly gone, no fever for four days, eating soft foods, stools normal again. Mild loose stool from the antibiotic, manageable.

Exam: afebrile, vitals as charted. Abdomen soft, minimal LLQ tenderness, no guarding.

Labs today: WBC back to normal. Creatinine at baseline after the CT contrast.

1. Sigmoid diverticulitis, uncomplicated, improving. Finish antibiotics. Advance diet as tolerated, fiber over time.
2. Colonoscopy: last one 2016. With a first CT-proven episode, I would like the colon looked at once he has recovered. Referral to GI.

documents.title: Colonoscopy Report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
COLONOSCOPY, 08/29/2024
Indication: CT-proven sigmoid diverticulitis 06/2024; prior colonoscopy 2016.
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care. Prep: good (BBPS 8).
Findings: scope advanced to the cecum, appendiceal orifice and ileocecal valve photographed. Scattered diverticula in the sigmoid colon. Mucosa otherwise normal throughout. No mass, no stricture, no polyps.
Impression: sigmoid diverticulosis. No evidence of neoplasm.
Recommendation: high-fiber diet. No further screening colonoscopy needed at his age unless new symptoms.

Gastroenterology

documents.title: Colonoscopy
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Tom, I read the colonoscopy report. Only diverticula in the sigmoid, no polyps or growths. That is reassuring after the June episode. More fiber over time; no more screening colonoscopies needed.

documents.title: Cardiology Discharge Summary
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 06/13/2025 via the emergency department; discharged 06/17/2025.
Principal diagnosis: inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
Secondary: contrast-induced nephropathy on CKD stage 3b.

Presentation: 72 year old man with diabetes and CKD who came in about two hours after the start of chest pain spreading into his left arm, with breathlessness and sweating. BP 160/90, HR 102, RR 22. Glucose high on arrival, consistent with his diabetes under stress. Baseline creatinine 1.8, eGFR 40. ECG: ST elevation in II, III and aVF. STEMI alert.

Course: emergent coronary angiography via right radial artery with limited contrast: occluded right coronary artery, treated with one drug-eluting stent with good result. Pain resolved in the lab. Echo 06/15: EF 50%, inferior hypokinesis. Creatinine rose to 2.6 on hospital day 2 after the contrast and was 2.2 at discharge, urine output preserved; metformin held 48 hours after contrast and then resumed. Uneventful telemetry.

Discharge medications:
- aspirin 81 mg daily (NEW)
- clopidogrel 75 mg daily (NEW), do not stop without talking to cardiology
- metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily (NEW)
- atorvastatin 40 mg daily
- lisinopril 20 mg daily
- hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily
- metformin 1000 mg twice daily
- pancrelipase with meals
- latanoprost both eyes at bedtime
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: PCP within 1 week with a BMP; cardiology in 8 weeks; cardiac rehabilitation referral placed.

Cardiology

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit: Inferior MI
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Transitional care visit. Discharge summary has not reached us; history from Tom and his hospital paperwork (medication list and the instruction sheet he brought).

Admitted 6/13 with an inferior STEMI, one stent to the right coronary artery. He was told the dye affected his kidneys and that he should have blood work. Home 6/17.

Since discharge: no chest pain, no dyspnea at rest, walking around the house and yard. A little lightheaded standing up fast the first two days, gone now. No bleeding or bruising. Taking all medicines; showed me the bottles.

Meds reconciled: aspirin 81, clopidogrel 75, metoprolol succinate 25 (all new), atorvastatin 40, lisinopril 20, HCTZ 12.5, metformin 1000 BID, pancrelipase, latanoprost.

Exam: vitals as charted. Right wrist access site healed, radial pulse good. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. No edema.

Labs: creatinine 2.0, down from what he was told in the hospital, still above his baseline of 1.8. Potassium normal. Hgb stable, platelets normal.

A/P:
1. Inferior STEMI, s/p drug-eluting stent to RCA. Dual antiplatelet therapy; reviewed that clopidogrel must not be stopped without cardiology. Cardiac rehab referral was placed by the hospital, he will call them. Cardiology in August.
2. Contrast-induced nephropathy on CKD 3b, improving. Recheck BMP in 6 to 8 weeks. Avoid NSAIDs, stay hydrated.
3. T2DM: metformin was held 48 h and resumed per his sheet.
4. HTN: BP fine on the regimen.
5. Records request for the discharge summary.

RTC 7 weeks.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 06/16/2026 through the ED; discharged 06/19/2026.
Diagnosis: acute pulmonary edema with severe hypertension.

Presentation: 73 year old man with type 2 diabetes, CKD stage 3, a history of contrast nephropathy, inferior MI with RCA stent (06/2025) and resected pancreatic cancer. While watching television in the evening he became suddenly, severely short of breath and began coughing up pink, frothy sputum. On arrival RR 30, BP 180/100, HR 110, SpO2 85% on room air. Crackles to the mid-lung fields on both sides, jugular venous pressure up, 2+ pitting edema of both legs. Creatinine 1.8, his baseline. BNP markedly elevated. Chest film: pulmonary edema with cephalization and septal lines. ECG: inferior ST elevation, unchanged from his 2025 tracing; no new ischemic change, catheterization not felt to be indicated.

Course: nitroglycerin infusion, IV furosemide and noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation in the ED, with rapid improvement; weaned to room air the next morning. Echocardiogram EF 50%, unchanged. Blood pressure controlled on his home regimen.

Discharge medications: furosemide 20 mg daily (NEW); aspirin 81 mg; clopidogrel 75 mg; metoprolol succinate 25 mg; atorvastatin 40 mg; lisinopril 20 mg; hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg; metformin 1000 mg twice daily; pancrelipase with meals; latanoprost both eyes at bedtime.
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: cardiology in 2 weeks; primary care.

Cardiology
